---
title: "Project 2: Heatwave analysis for Italy (R version)"
output: html_notebook
---

R equivalent of the Python notebook `project2_italy_heatwave.ipynb`. Analysis of the summer 2022 heatwave in Italy: ERA5 2-metre temperature (Copernicus CDS API), weekly all-cause mortality (World Mortality Dataset by Karlinsky & Kobak), a simple time-series model of excess mortality, and a binned scatter plot of the mortality-temperature relationship.

**Requirements:** see the project `README.md`. A Copernicus CDS account (personal access token) is needed to download ERA5, and `world_mortality.csv` must be placed in `data/`. Expected layout: this notebook lives in `R/`; the ERA5 NetCDF files are downloaded to `../data/era5/` (not tracked by git).

## Task 1 : Generate the ERA5 data extract for Italy

Task 1.1: Generate the ERA5 data extract for Italy using the API of daily-hourly data starting in 2015. As a consequence, the reference period for our analysis will be 2015-2020, when we assess the situation in the summer of 2022. Recall that the coordinates are (anti-clockwise): [N,W,S,E]. The bounding box for Italy is [46,9,37,18.5].

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)    # dates, ISO weeks
library(ecmwfr)       # Copernicus CDS API
library(ncdf4)        # read the NetCDF files
library(sf)           # coastlines for the map
library(rnaturalearth)
library(aweek)        # start date of a week (equivalent of get_date)
library(binsreg)      # binned scatter plot

# Output folder (relative path; the .nc files are not tracked by git)
DATADIR <- "../data/era5"
dir.create(DATADIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Run once: store your CDS personal access token (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/how-to-api)
# wf_set_key(key = "<your CDS personal access token>")
```

```{r}
# Download year by year to stay within the CDS API request limits
for (year in 2015:2024) {

  target <- sprintf("Italy_%d.nc", year)

  # Skip the years already downloaded
  if (file.exists(file.path(DATADIR, target))) next
  message("Downloading ", year, "...")

  request <- list(
    dataset_short_name = "reanalysis-era5-single-levels",
    product_type = "reanalysis",
    variable     = "2m_temperature",
    year         = as.character(year),
    month        = sprintf("%02d", 1:12),
    day          = sprintf("%02d", 1:31),
    time         = sprintf("%02d:00", 0:23),
    area         = c(46, 9, 37, 18.5),        # Italy bounding box [N, W, S, E]
    data_format  = "netcdf",
    download_format = "unarchived",
    target       = target
  )

  wf_request(request, path = DATADIR, transfer = TRUE)
}
message("Download completed")
```

```{r}
# Loading and preparing the ERA5 temperature data.
# The data were downloaded year by year to comply with CDS API limits:
# each file is read, converted to Celsius and averaged by day, then the years are stacked.

# Convert the "valid_time" variable of a NetCDF file into POSIXct
read_valid_time <- function(nc) {
  v     <- ncvar_get(nc, "valid_time")
  units <- ncatt_get(nc, "valid_time", "units")$value
  mult  <- c(seconds = 1, minutes = 60, hours = 3600, days = 86400)[sub(" since.*", "", units)]
  as.POSIXct(sub(".*since ", "", units), tz = "UTC") + v * mult
}

files <- list.files(DATADIR, pattern = "^Italy_[0-9]{4}\\.nc$", full.names = TRUE)

daily_list <- lapply(files, function(f) {
  nc <- nc_open(f)
  on.exit(nc_close(nc))

  t2m_C <- ncvar_get(nc, "t2m") - 273.15   # Conversion to Celsius (dims: longitude, latitude, time)
  lon   <- ncvar_get(nc, "longitude")
  lat   <- ncvar_get(nc, "latitude")
  day   <- as.Date(read_valid_time(nc))

  # Daily aggregation: group the hours by date (Year-Month-Day) and take the mean
  m     <- matrix(t2m_C, nrow = length(lon) * length(lat))   # cells x hours
  daily <- rowsum(t(m), group = day) / as.vector(table(day))   # days x cells
  list(daily = daily, lon = lon, lat = lat)
})

lon <- daily_list[[1]]$lon
lat <- daily_list[[1]]$lat
year_month_day_mean <- do.call(rbind, lapply(daily_list, `[[`, "daily"))   # days x cells
dates <- as.Date(rownames(year_month_day_mean))

dim(year_month_day_mean)   # number of days x number of grid cells
range(dates)
```

Task 1.2: Then aggregate hourly local data for the week, and then aggregate the local measures. Display the map. Finally, write the data to disk as a csv file.

```{r}
# Latitude weights (cosine of latitude), one weight per grid cell.
# Note: this is a mean over the requested bounding box, including sea and neighboring
# regions; no Italy land mask is applied in this version.
weights <- rep(cos(lat * pi / 180), each = length(lon))

# Weighted mean over the grid for each day
Italy_t2m <- as.vector(year_month_day_mean %*% weights) / sum(weights)
```

```{r}
# Extraction for August 3rd, 2022
target_date <- as.Date("2022-08-03")

map_0308 <- expand_grid(latitude = lat, longitude = lon) %>%
  arrange(latitude, longitude) %>%
  mutate(t2m = as.vector(year_month_day_mean[as.character(target_date), ]))
```

```{r, fig.width=16, fig.height=8}
dir.create("pics", showWarnings = FALSE)

coast <- ne_coastline(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

p_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = map_0308, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = t2m)) +
  geom_sf(data = coast, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, name = "temperature (°C)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(9, 18.5), ylim = c(37, 46), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Mean temperatures on 03.08.2022", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16), panel.grid = element_line(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70"))

ggsave("pics/map_Italy_August2022_2.png", p_map, width = 16, height = 8)
p_map
```

### Aggregation of weekly mean temperatures

```{r}
# 1. Daily series of the weighted mean temperature
df_italy <- tibble(date = dates, t2m = Italy_t2m)

# 2. Extract Year and (ISO) Week from the date
# 3. Group by Year and Week to get the weekly average
# Note: as in the Python version, "year" is the calendar year and "week" the ISO week,
# so the days of an ISO week that straddle two calendar years form two groups.
weekly_temp <- df_italy %>%
  mutate(year = isoyear(date), week = isoweek(date)) %>%
  group_by(year, week) %>%
  summarise(t2m = mean(t2m), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    jan4 = as.Date(paste0(year, "-01-04")),
    start_date = jan4 - days(wday(jan4, week_start = 1) - 1) + weeks(week - 1)
  ) %>%
  select(-jan4)

# 4. Write the data to disk as a csv file
write_csv(weekly_temp, "../data/Italy_week_temperature.csv")

weekly_temp
```

## Task 1.3

Load your csv-file of the temperature data, and visualise this temperature data. Consider the summer of 2022 starting in June and finishing end of August.

```{r}
# Load the csv file
weekly_temp <- read_csv("../data/Italy_week_temperature.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Filtering data for Summer 2022
summer_2022_temp <- weekly_temp %>%
  filter(year == 2022, between(week, 22, 35))

summer_2022_temp
```

```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
# Plot the series on the Monday starting each ISO week.
ggplot(weekly_temp, aes(x = start_date, y = t2m)) +
  # 3. Add the grey area for summer 2022
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date("2022-06-01"), xmax = as.Date("2022-08-31"),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "darkgrey", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_date(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Time evolution of average temperature (t2m) from 2015 to 2024",
       x = "week", y = "t2m") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)
```

## 2 The mortality data

Task 2.1. Use of the World Mortality Dataset compiled by Ariel Karlinsky and Dmitry Kobak that records all-cause mortality at a weekly level. Filter Italy, which has iso3c code "ITA".

```{r}
# Loading and previewing the mortality dataset
world_mort <- read_csv("../data/world_mortality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(world_mort)
```

```{r}
# Filtering Italy data and cleaning the mortality dataset
# (start_date: first day of the ISO week, equivalent of get_date)
set_week_start("Monday")

mortality <- world_mort %>%
  filter(iso3c == "ITA") %>%                                   # filter
  select(-c(iso3c, country_name, time_unit)) %>%               # select(-c(...))
  rename(mortality = deaths, week = time) %>%                  # rename
  mutate(start_date = get_date(week = week, year = year))      # start of the week

mortality
```

## 3 A simple time-series model of excess mortality

Task 3: Next, estimate a simple time-series model of excess mortality for the period before 2020-03-01, which only considers a linear year effect and week fixed effects. Then use the model to predict mortality for the summer of 2022, and compute the measure of excess mortality (i.e. observed - predicted weekly mortality from all causes).

```{r}
# 1. Split train (before March 2020) / test (summer 2022)
train <- mortality %>% filter(start_date < as.Date("2020-03-01"))
summer_2022 <- mortality %>% filter(year == 2022, between(week, 22, 35))

# 2. Fit the model: linear year effect + week fixed effects (one dummy per week)
model <- lm(mortality ~ year + factor(week), data = train)

# 3. Predict summer 2022
summer_2022$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = summer_2022)

# 4. Compute excess mortality (Observed - Predicted)
summer_2022$excess_mortality <- summer_2022$mortality - summer_2022$predicted

# Total excess mortality
total_excess <- sum(summer_2022$excess_mortality)
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
# Plot the excess mortality curve
ggplot(summer_2022, aes(x = start_date, y = excess_mortality, colour = "excess deaths")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("excess deaths" = "#FF2E00"), name = NULL) +
  # Display the months on the x-axis (Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep)
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(title = "Italy : Excess deaths", x = "date", y = "death count") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 22, hjust = 0),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
cat(sprintf("Estimated total excess mortality (summer 2022): %.0f deaths\n", total_excess))
```

## 4 The mortality and temperature relationship

Task 4: Finally consider the (potential all-cause) mortality and temperature relationship using a bin scatter plot.

```{r}
# 1. Merge the mortality data with the weekly temperature on year and week
#    (the weekly_temp "date" column is only used for plotting and is dropped)
# 2. We keep only rows where the year is NOT equal to 2024, and where a temperature is available
df_merged <- mortality %>%
  left_join(select(weekly_temp, start_date, t2m), by = "start_date") %>%
  filter(year != 2024, !is.na(t2m))
```

```{r}
# Generate the binned scatter plot
# y: dependent variable "mortality"; x: independent variable "t2m"
# nbins: number of bins
# line = c(1, 0): the first 1 is the degree of the polynomial (1 = linear / straight line),
#                 the second 0 means 0 constraints on derivatives at the knots (creates the gaps)
est <- binsreg(
  y = df_merged$mortality, x = df_merged$t2m,
  data = df_merged, nbins = 10, line = c(1, 0)
)
est$bins_plot +
  labs(x = "Bounding-box mean temperature (degrees C)", y = "Weekly all-cause deaths") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)
```
